about.title: Ross Slip & Fall and Premises Liability Claims
about.longDescription: Ross is a small, quiet town, but that doesn't mean falls don't happen — a cracked sidewalk near Ross Commons, a wet floor left unmarked in a Sir Francis Drake Boulevard storefront, or uneven pavement along Loma Linda Avenue can all lead to serious injury. Under California law, a property owner or manager can be held responsible when they knew, or reasonably should have known, about a dangerous condition and didn't fix it or warn visitors. Because Ross is compact and many properties are privately owned or managed by small businesses and homeowners' associations, figuring out who's legally responsible for a hazard can take some digging. If you were hurt on someone else's property, LawProactive can connect you with an independent attorney who understands how these cases are built, from documenting the hazard to tracking down surveillance footage before it's erased. There's no cost to get connected, and no obligation to move forward.

whyChoose.title: What Matters in a Ross Premises Liability Case

items.title: Proving Notice
items.desc: California requires showing the property owner knew, or should have known, about the hazard and failed to address it. An attorney can help gather evidence, like maintenance logs or prior complaints, that supports this.

items.title: Acting Before Evidence Disappears
items.desc: Surveillance footage from a store or common area near Ross Commons is often overwritten within days or weeks. Preserving that footage early can make a real difference in a claim.

items.title: Understanding Comparative Fault
items.desc: California uses pure comparative fault, so even if you're partly blamed for not noticing a hazard, you may still recover a reduced amount. An attorney can help present your side clearly and fairly.

items.question: How long do I have to file a slip and fall claim in Ross?
items.answer: Generally, California gives you two years from the date of the fall to file a premises liability lawsuit. That window is shorter if the property involved is owned by a public entity, so it helps to get an evaluation sooner rather than later.

items.question: What if I was partly at fault for not seeing the hazard?
items.answer: California's pure comparative fault rule means you can still pursue compensation even if you share some blame, though your recovery may be reduced by your percentage of fault. It's still worth having your situation reviewed.

items.question: I fell near Ross Common or on a walkway along Sir Francis Drake Boulevard — who's responsible?
items.answer: Responsibility depends on who owns or manages the specific property or walkway where you fell, which in a small town like Ross can involve a private owner, business tenant, or local association. An independent attorney can help identify the right party and gather documentation before it's lost.
